speechtext: I would ask all Hon. Members who are not participating in the debate to please clear the Chamber.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your attempt to have Hon. Members carry on their conversations outside the House so that we continue this discussion on refugee policy.
The motion before the House today asks the House to condemn the Government's refugee policy for its failing badly to uphold Canada's proud and humane record for refugee assistance. It goes on to deplore the Government's refusal to assure refugee claimants, in its new legislation, full accessibility to, and a non-adversarial hearing before, an independent refugee board. In addition, the motion urges the Government to establish a fair, accessible and efficient refugee determination system, and the details are put before the House for the consideration of the Government.
In order to discuss Canadian policy on refugees we must first put Canada into a world context with respect to refugees. As most Hon. Members know, there is a growing tragedy of refugees and misplaced persons throughout the world. This has been due in part to the incidence of regional wars, civil conflicts and revolutions throughout the world.
As of February, 1986, there was on record, since 1945, 120 regional and local wars resulting in 19 million deaths. Many people talk about the last war and they refer to the war in 1945.
As 1 just pointed out, since 1945 there have been 120 regional and local wars resulting in 19 million deaths. Two-thirds of those deaths were among civilians, and 16 million of them were in the Third World.
In addition to the large number of deaths resulting from regional and local wars, the United Nations estimates that there are between 15 million and 20 million refugees in the world. About three million of them are Afghans and about two million of them are Palestinians. They include refugees from Indo-China, Iran, Central America, and Latin America.
As citizens of the world, not only citizens of Canada, we must ask who will take care of these refugees? Is Canada

May 12, 1987
Supply
doing its job, or are we shifting the burden to someone else? Are we doing our share?
As Elon. Members know, Canada signed the 1951 International Convention on Refugees in 1969, according to which convention we agreed to receive refugees as defined by the treaty and our law. In order to do that, we set up the Refugee Status Advisory Committee. While the process might have been very acceptable in 1969 when we passed the legislation, while it might have been adequate in the first place, it was certainly found to be inadequate with the large growing number of refugees throughout the world who were coming to our shores in the early 1980s.
As a result of the growing number of applications, the Government appointed the Plaut Commission to advise on how to deal with the enormous backlog of applications which was developing and how to put in place a new refugee determination process.
I think at one point during 1985 we had over 20,000 applicants waiting from two to three years to have their refugee status determined by the process. Not only was it a major problem for those who were waiting to have their determination as refugees decided, it also unfortunately encouraged a growing number of false refugees.
What was happening was that people were coming into the country and claiming refugee status. Since they had to wait two to three years to have their status determined, often they were marrying Canadians and having children in Canada. In other words, they were becoming well established here. Even if it were found after the two-year period that they were not really refugees, it became very difficult to send them out of the country with all the ties they had developed within that time. However, that process also encouraged more false refugees because they knew once they arrived here and made their application, by the time they were turned down they would also be considered as cases which should be allowed to stay, on compassionate grounds.
As I stated, the former Liberal Government was concerned about the problem. It appointed the Plaut Commission in 1983 to advise on a new refugee determination process and a system to deal with the backlog. Rabbi Plaut reported in April, 1985, to the new Conservative Government. The report was referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. The standing committee studied the report, listened to the evidence of witnesses, and heard from many non-governmental organizations which deal with refugees in Canada. The committee reported in November and December, 1985. It put out two reports. One proposed a new refugee determination process which was based upon the Plaut report, but not quite similar to it. Its second report concerned what to do with the large backlog of refugees. The committee recommended a fast and fair process which I thought was supportable and could have been acceptable to the House of Commons and to many refugee support groups in Canada.
In part the Government responded to these reports in May, 1986, and promised legislation later in 1986. As we know, we did not get that legislation in 1986. We only got it in the last couple of weeks.
During that period of time all the problems to which I have referred galloped along-the growing number of refugee applications and the large number of fraudulent or false claims.
In order to support the measures it put into place on February 20 of this year, prior to the Bill to which many of us have referred, although it is not under debate today, I believe the Government gave a false impression of the refugee situation in Canada. It gave the impression that the numbers of refugees at our doors were much higher than they have been historically and that, consequently, we had to bring in harsh measures, which I believe were unfair, to deal with the situation.
If we look at the facts, I do not think we can justify either the measures of February 20 or the legislation. I should like to refer to some of the situations in past years. While the Government has argued that the type of legislation before us is necessary because of the large backlog in the number of refugee applications, I should put on record the fact that we had much larger refugee movements into Canada in previous years.
In 1982, just a few years ago, we had three special movements into Canada in addition to the regular flow of refugees. The regular flow in that year was 16,908. In addition, we had a special movement of Polish refugees amounting to 9,344; a special movement of Iranian refugees amounting to 2,501; and a special movement of Salvadoran refugees amounting to 3,024. Those special movements add up to 14,869 refugees in addition to the regular quota.
If we look at the period of time from 1976 to 1979, Canada admitted 11,321 Lebanese refugees as a result of the war in their country. In the period following the Vietnamese war in 1978, we admitted 9,060 Vietnamese refugees. Following the overthrow of the Allende Government in Chile, Canada admitted over 7,000 refugees from Chile and Argentina. In 1973 we admitted over 7,000 Ugandan Asians. In 1969 we admitted 11,943 Czechoslovakian refugees. After the Hungarian revolution in 1957 we admitted 37,149 Hungarians.
I put these figures on the record to indicate that the number of refugees we now have applying for status in Canada is not unusual. We have admitted great numbers of refugees into Canada in past years since the Second World War. These people are now in Canada.
Who in this House would maintain that these refugees have caused us any difficulty? Who would complain today of the Hungarians who came in 1957, the Czechs who came in 1969, the Ugandan Asians in 1973, the Chileans in 1979; and we could go on and on-the Vietnamese, the Lebanese and the
May 12, 1987

Poles in 1982? These people have come to Canada and have made a valuable contribution. I do not think anybody regrets the fact that they were admitted as special movements of refugees, or suggests that we would have been better off if we had had special measures which would have prevented them from coming to our shores.
This could be said of all immigrants, but it could also be said of refugees. Refugees and immigrants are, for the most part, great contributors to the country. They are consumers. They buy food and clothing. They need housing, education and health care. Some people maintain that immigrants and refugees take jobs away from us. I argue that they provide jobs for Canadians, not only to the extent that they are consumers but also because many of them are innovative entrepreneurs who put together enterprises and hire many other Canadians.
We have finally had put before us Bill C-55, which is the Government's response to the Plaut report and the reports of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I do not consider Bill C-55 an adequate response. I support the wording in the resolution before this House today, that that policy must be condemned.
In the first place it must be condemned because, according to the provisions of that Bill, access to the refugee determination process will not be universal. Both the Plaut report and the report of the Standing Committee suggested that any process we put in place should be universal. In other words, it should be accessible to all of those who claim refugee status. If a person comes to Canada claiming to be a refugee, he or she should have a chance to prove his case.
What do we have with Bill C-55? We have provisions whereby once a person claims to be a refugee and is asked from what country he came, if he states that he has come from what is considered a safe country, then he is immediately sent back to that country. He is not given an opportunity to put his case before the refugee determination board, or whatever the new name for it might be. He is not given an opportunity to put all the facts before an independent tribunal to show that he really is a refugee. Because he comes from what is considered to be a safe country, he is immediately sent back without access to a tribunal to hear his case.
Who will define what a safe country is and who will set out a list of these said countries? We do not at present have in the Bill a definition of a safe country. It is simply referred to, and we are told that the Government will provide a list of countries it considers safe, countries to which people can be returned without giving the individual a chance to have his or her case heard. We can speculate on which countries will be included in the list.
I heard a program on the CBC the other night. People from the CBC telephoned individuals working in a refugee movement in the United States. They described the new Canadian legislation to the Americans and asked them whether they considered the United States as a safe country for Guatemalan
Supply
and Salvadoran refugees. In other words, they said that if Canada listed the United States as a safe country, then as a Salvadoran refugee who had come from the United States would be sent back there. The Americans were asked whether, in that case the United States was safe for Salvadoran and Guatemalan refugees? Their answer was no. They said most Salvadoran and Guatemalan refugees who come to the United States are not acceptable as refugees in the United States.
We can speculate about which countries the Cabinet will consider safe countries under this legislation. But how will the Government define a safe country?
As we all know, the conditions that give rise to the refugee phenomenon often come about suddenly. There is suddenly a coups d'etat in a country; suddenly new repressive measures are put in place and people flee overnight. That happened in the Hungarian revolution of 1957, to which I referred, in the Czech situation in 1969, during the Vietnamese war, in Lebanon and so on. You cannot predict in advance the conditions in countries which will oblige people to flee as refugees. Nor can you predict that these situations will change from day to day, from week to week, or from month to month. As well, what might be a safe country for one group of refugees may not be a safe country for another group. Maybe the United States is a safe country for people fleeing from Poland, but it is not a safe country for people fleeing from Salvador.
We condemn this new process being suggested to the House of Commons and to the people of Canada as one that is not acceptable. It is not acceptable because it does not provide universal access to an independent tribunal so that a person claiming refugee status can have a full and an impartial hearing of his or her claim, after which somebody can say yes, you really are a refugee in accordance with our law and the international treaty, or no, you are not really a refugee. What we are doing is sending certain people away without a hearing because they come from what is called a safe country.
We have other objections to the legislation. We object to the fact that the preliminary panel to hear these refugee applications is not made up of two people from the refugee side of the Department. It is made up of one person from the immigration side and another person from the refugee side. In our resolution we suggest a system somewhat similar to what was suggested in the standing committee's report.
We need in Canada a fair system to deal with refugee applications, a fast system in order to deter and prevent fraudulent refugees, a system that is open to all of those who claim refugee status, a system that would allow a person to apply for refugee status from anywhere, from within Canada or from without, and a system which has a fair appeal process. As I said at the beginning, the refugee problem is a human problem of vast dimensions. We in Canada who are relatively well off should not shirk our responsibility or pass the buck concerning this issue. We did not shirk it before. Certainly we can do something again.

May 12, 1987
Supply

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member raised on his own behalf, and on behalf of many who want it, the concept of open access to an independent convention refugee determination board member. The claimant has that; every person will have the opportunity to demonstrate whether his life, limb or liberty is at risk. The Hon. Member wants to send out some kind of scare in the community that the adjudicator and the member of the independent convention refugee determination board have no discretion.
We have clearly said that the claimant will be put through two tests. The first test involves objective criteria. Does the person have refugee status elsewhere? Can he be returned to a safe third country? Some manifestly unfounded claims will be shown. If a person has recently been rejected from Canada or is presently under a deportation order, those facts must be examined using the same criteria.
The second test is a low-threshold, low-standard credibility test. The individual can demonstrate his fear of going back to where we want to send him. If he has lived a sufficient length of time in a country or has legal status, that will be taken into consideration. If one of those two people with discretion feels that there is a shred of a chance that this man fears for his very life, limb, liberty or security, he will be referred to a hearing within 10 days. To me that is discretion.
The Hon. Member has placed particular emphasis on what a safe third country will mean when the Cabinet sets forward such a list. I have tried to tell Hon. Members that because this is a life and death matter, the criteria will be very stringent. We will examine the human rights record of the countries in question. Before a country will be put on the safe country list, it will have to show a record of refugee protection and of protection of all nationals of any country. There will be the widest consultation and we will seek the best advice possible in addition to the advice of our own officials, those of the Department of External Affairs and the documentation centre that will be set up. We understand how important that is for these individuals.
We have put into place a system that is quick and expeditious but provides for quality hearings before independent board members. I believe that that is fair, no matter what the Hon. Member wants to say about further levels of appeal. Given a poor decision, a reviewing body that does not have a chance to feel and to sense the fear of an individual must be weighed against an open, independent hearing before an independent member of the refugee board.

Mr. Speaker, I thought this period was for questions or short comments, not for alternative speeches. Nevertheless, the Minister said that all those who claim refugee status will be given a fair hearing in this new process. It seems to me that the Minister has not read the Bill. Clause 48.1 which appears on page 13 of the Bill indicates that a person who claims to be a Convention refugee is not eligible to have the claim determined by the refugee division if the
claimant came to Canada from a country that has been described as a safe third country. There is in the legislation a barrier against a whole group of people who claim to be refugees if they came from what is considered to be a safe third country. They do not even get a chance to put the facts of their cases before the refugee process.
The preliminary panel will ask such an individual if he claims to be a refugee, and he will say yes. The panel will ask him from which country he has just come, and if he says he has just come from the United States, that is it, too bad. The United States is on the list of safe countries, so back he goes to the United States. The fact that he is from Salvador and not from Poland or from Vietnam and not from Czechoslovakia does not matter. The United States is on the list of safe countries so the refugee does not have one more word to say.
If that is the case, how can the Minister say that he is putting in place a process under which a refugee applicant will have every opportunity to put before the refugee determination board all the facts with respect to his particular case? It is true that if he does not come from a safe country and if some of the other conditions are met, then he has a chance to demonstrate his case. We as members of the Liberal Party are saying that that process does not afford universal access. If we are to be fair to refugees, we should have a fast, efficient and fair system but one that is universal so everyone who claims to be a refugee would have a chance to put all the facts before the board, and that is not the case right now.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague spoke very passionately about the situation that exists in the world and listed a number of very disconcerting facts and figures concerning upheavals throughout the world. As I see it, another problem with the concept of a safe third country is the time the Government will take to react to new uprisings, to new human rights abuses, to new geopolitical circumstances that could arise literally overnight.
I wonder what the Hon. Member thinks about the lag time it would take for a government bureaucracy to change its list so that people would not be sent back to a hot spot that would otherwise be on the safe country list. Has the Hon. Member any thoughts on that particular controversy and the practical problems that will be created for bona fide refugees escaping areas of persecution without being recognized because the safe country list has not been modified?

Mr. Speaker, I was a member of Cabinet for seven years and I know how slowly these things move. The Hon. Minister must be aware of that as well. This legislation was promised in May, 1986, and it took until May, 1987 to get it before the House. It went through the various cabinet committees and back and forth to interdepartmental committees, I suppose.
No matter how good the intentions of the Minister are, and I know the Minister is of good faith, things do change in the world. I cited the examples of the Hungarian and Czechoslovakian revolutions and the Polish Solidarity situation, all
May 12, 1987

things which led to sudden and vast movements of refugees. We cannot always predict where these things will happen and which country will be safe and which will not. As well, some countries are safe for some but not for others and the legislation does not provide for that.
In committee, we asked the Minister if he would give a definition of a safe third country before we voted on the Bill so that we would be able to better judge the proposed legislation. I think he said he would try to do that. I cannot recall his exact words now, but they were not altogether negative and may have even been positive. In any case, we still insist on having a definition, as do most Canadian refugee support groups.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to rise this afternoon. I would like to begin by clearing up some of the confusion that exists in the community. Last Thursday, I took the unusual step of asking to be replaced on the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration because I believed that at a meeting held on April 14, my role as the administrator of that committee had been compromised and that that role needed to be re-established because of the important work of the committee. People have asked whether or not I resigned for other reasons relating to the refugee Bill or to unemployment insurance matters. I simply want to assure the House and the community that the action I took was exactly as described and for the reasons described.
If there has been a bonus for me personally as it affects my role in relation to this Bill, it is that it has given me a bit more time to work on it. I do not have to do other things that were indeed time-consuming and perhaps less important in my own mind than refugee legislation for the future.
I must confess that I have a certain feeling of unease with regard to this debate. That unease begins with the fact that this is an Opposition Day motion. A motion on an Opposition Day tends to cause us to draw Party lines. When we are dealing with a matter of life and death, and that is truly what we do when we debate the subject of refugees, we are attempting to help this nation define its own sense of morality concerning those unfortunate people who have become refugees in our modern world. I would hope that we do not continue to discuss this situation and the legislation itself from the perspective of partisan politics. It is not necessary for all Members of this House to agree on what might be the best process, just as it is not necessary for all Members to agree on the capital punishment debate. However, when we are dealing with morality, we hear the knowledge and opinion of those who serve this House and those who elect them. The refugee issue is a moral issue.
I was particularly disturbed, I guess, by the pro forma words of introduction to this resolution. It starts: "That this House condemns the Government's refugee policy-". I wonder if all Members really know what is being condemned. There is a sense in some quarters in this country that Progressive
Supply
Conservatives feel less strongly about the issue of refugees, that perhaps they are less humanitarian in orientation. Some quarters are perhaps too moral and others perhaps not moral enough. Yet I think it is sometimes wise to stand back from our stereotypes and look at performance.
In my adult lifetime there have been three Progressive Conservative Prime Ministers of this country. The first one I knew was the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker. He was Prime Minister in 1959 when the UN declared the Year of the Refugee. Under his leadership and that of his Government this country opened its doors to some especially disadvantaged refugees. That Government put in place a government-sponsored program that would help the socially or medically handicapped refugee. There were under private sector sponsorship special programs for refugees suffering from tuberculosis. That was a leadership role in the world community motivated by the finest of instincts, that of providing help to those in the world community who needed it the most.
In more recent times the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) was Prime Minister of this country for a very brief period of time. Of all the public policies initiated by his Government perhaps the best remembered and longest lasting in its impact on this nation was the leadership provided when the world was faced with the boat people crisis in southeast Asia. This country led the world with its quickness, sureness and openness in making its contribution to solving that crisis in a far off corner of the world.
What about the present Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Government, in office for two years and eight months? In the last year of the previous Government we brought 14,000 people to this country under refugee landings and designated classes. By 1986, the second full year of this Government, that had increased 40 per cent to 19,000 people.
I think those actions, more clearly and eloquently than anything else I can say, speak to the policy of this Government and its commitment to refugees. It is a better record, I suggest, than that of the previous Government. On each and every occasion where we have had a change in Government in this country, Progressive Conservative Prime Ministers and their Cabinets have made a more open, more generous and more secure commitment to refugees. That may be because so many of the members of our caucus and our Cabinet can trace their own roots back to a refugee movement at some time in the not too distant past.
What is a refugee? Sometimes we tend to throw terms around without pausing to consider who we have in mind. As I approach legislative and policy-making tasks in this Chamber I find it helpful to focus on perhaps one single human being who to some extent typifies the subject matter of a given policy. I learned a long time ago that when Government acts, it advantages some people in society and disadvantages others. Who is it we wish to advantage through our refugee policy? At the head of my list are those who are being persecuted, who face torture or death if they remain in their country of origin. They had no choice, they had to flee. In most cases they had to

May 12, 1987
Supply
leave behind their family, their worldly possessions, their educational credentials and their work experience. They had to leave all that behind and flee. If in doing so they end up on or within the borders of Canada, then morally we have no choice. We must accept their petition. They must have a chance to be heard, to tell their story. They must have a chance to persuade us that they are genuine refugees.
These are not people who, for the most part, if given freedom of choice, would choose to come to Canada and make their life here. When we talk about a refugee, we are generally talking about someone who loves his or her country of origin. They would like nothing more in life than to be able to stay in that country, make their lives, raise their families, build their careers and make their contribution there. Circumstances have forced them out. Disagreements with their Government, or accidents of birth reflected in their skin colour or their religion. Those things are viewed by some in some countries as inappropriate qualities, as excuses to persecute, torture and execute. If any of us in this Chamber faced those circumstances we also would attempt to flee.
Having fled, what happens then? Do we spend a lifetime in a refugee camp, or do we attempt to find a country where we can start again, raise a family and make a contribution? Those are the kind of people all of us should have in mind when we talk about refugees and look at Bill C-55.
When someone arrives in Canada today he is given an examination under oath by an immigration officer who is not trained in refugee matters but in immigration law, policing if you like. There is an independent body which reviews the transcripts of those hearings. If you take the time and trouble to review those transcripts you will see that those interviews were not always conducted with great skill. The transcripts are not always helpful in deciding whether or not a case is that of a true refugee. Nevertheless, the law requires that the transcripts be read and a recommendation be made to the Minister of Immigration.
It is only at the third major stage of the immigration appeal board that the claimants have the right to appear in person and tell their own story to a decision-maker. That body hears appeals on all kinds of immigration matters; deportation hearings, family class immigration, and so on. Refugee cases are only a part of the workload. These are not expert people who devote their full time to the consideration of refugee matters.
The next level of appeal is before the Federal Court of Canada, and those people are not experts either. We have no body in this country today which is expert in refugee matters and sits down face to face with a refugee claimant and reaches a decision about whether or not the claim to the protection of Canada is justifiable.
We must have such a body as quickly as possible and put in place as securely as possible. To do otherwise is to continue the
present system which is backward and punishes the true refugee. People who arrive at our border after having gone through a period of imprisonment, torture or persecution take their place in line with thousands of bogus claimants.
When the Government took office, it was taking three or four years to decide whether someone was a refugee. After having come out of a dungeon and being tortured, people arrive on the shores of freedom and it takes three to four years to make a decision on whether they deserve the protection of this country. That is inhumane and insane. That is the system today. We must all work together with the resources of Canada to do something more sane, sensible and better for refugees.
Those of us who have studied this matter in committee know that there are a variety of opinions on it. We understand that this is an extremely difficult area of law. It was naive of anyone in this country to assume that legislation brought into the House would be letter-perfect in all the fine print. I suggest that it was beyond the capability of the drafters to produce such a document. People skilled in legal drafting are not necessarily skilled in the subject matter in which they are drafting.
That is why the process of debate exists in the Parliament of Canada. That is why in committee we call witnesses and ask the best brains and most knowledgeable groups in the country to help us understand where the fine print is in accord with the principles and where it is not so that we can change the fine print where it is necessary to do so.
We have come a long way since the parliamentary committee reported in November, 1985. The Bill before us entitles every single claimant to a personal appearance before a member of the board within a week of arrival. Surely that is beneficial to legitimate refugee claimants. If that is a hardship for the bogus claimant, so be it. That is probably good because we do not want the resources of this nation going to the bogus claimant. Our resources should go to the legitimate refugee claimant. Any true refugee will have no fear of an appearance before a member of that expert body who is steeped in refugee matters, has a feel for them and knowledge of them.
We must ensure that the Minister's expression of intent appears in the fine print. If it is not now there, let us put it there, but let us have that initial decision-making. It is analogous to all parts of Canadian law. The preliminary hearing to decide whether the matter should proceed to trial is a well-known and honourable tradition in the British judicial system. That is all we have at stage one. We want to determine whether there is any reason at all to suspect that an individual needs the protection of Canada. If there is the slightest suspicion that they might, they go to stage two for a full oral hearing before a two-person panel.
Surely that is as it should be. If we want to give effect to our humanitarian traditions and act morally in relation to these people, let us put some resources into that stage, let us have a high-quality oral hearing and an appeal. Contained within this
May 12, 1987

legislation is the principle of a lot of Canadians who will work part-time as jurists to help us make this decision. Within that mechanism is a need for quality control. We cannot have a decision made in Elalifax on the same basis as one made in Vancouver or downtown Toronto. Inherent in that knowledge of administrative systems is the notion that decisions made by panels will have to be examined by someone, in whole or in part.
I say to the NGO community, as I said before, that in any decent piece of legislation we need the certitude that a mistake made by a panel can be corrected when need be. That is not synonymous with a formalized review, a 100 per cent appeal of every decision made. If we care about the persecuted who come to our shores, we need a high quality system and the certitude that on the rare occasions when we make a mistake we will have the power to correct it.
I say to Members of this House from all three Parties and to the community at large that this is a time for co-operation. The resources are inherent in the legislation. If it needs fixing and we have the wisdom to fix it, let us do so. Let us not get stuck as we did with the previous law. Let us not have a system which blocks but, rather, one which does the job. That system is inherent in the nature of this Bill. Let us work together to produce as good a Bill as our collective wisdom can provide.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset, let me say that I and, I believe, all Members appreciated the tenor of the Hon. Member's very deeply felt concerns on the question of refugee legislation. I might add that while I regret that he has resigned as chairman, and perhaps I differed with him on the issue over which he resigned, it should be on the record that as Chairman of the Standing Committee reviewing the refugee determination legislation he was at the forefront of some very progressive thinking. I hope that some of the things he and the committee represent will come to bear on the Government and the Cabinet.
The Member said that we will never have an ideal refugee system, just as we will never have an ideal society. I concur with those remarks and in fact suggested the very same thing in my speech. However, we must also realize that it goes beyond suggesting that the bureaucracy cannot draft everything in an ideal context. We must also focus our attention on the political will that will dictate what the bureaucracy drafts.
We have gone through a two and a half year consultation period, listening to some of the major tenets that were put forward by a number of non-governmental organizations, church organizations and our own committee. There were a number of common denominators in many of those recommendations, one of which was full accessibility to a proper oral hearing on the merits of those claims by a proper refugee decision-making body.
The Minister stated that the provision in this Bill does not represent a pre-screening stage at the various border points. I
Supply
disagree with him very strongly, as do a number of NGOs, I believe. If there is a pre-screening process that is rooted in a safe third country concept, both of which were hotly denied and rejected by the consultation process, one must wonder why the Government put those in place. While we will never have a system that is completely flawless, I think it is also irresponsible that the Government would put those in place after a consultation period of two and a half years.
The Hon. Member was involved in the process and the committee was very much opposed to any pre-screening apparatus. Therefore, what does the Member think of that prescreening stage and its being rooted in a third safe country concept, problems which he heard articulated earlier?

Mr. Speaker, I will attempt to respond to the Hon. Member. I see the pre-screening process as being in accordance with the committee's assertion that there should be universal access to a decision-making body that is the country's sole expert body on refugee matters. The Minister asserted time and time again in the House that it is Cabinet's will that every claimant be given face-to-face access to that body, in a hearing atmosphere where questions can be asked and information exchanged. There will not be the necessity at that point to document the case fully but simply to ensure that the presentation is sufficient to persuade the officer that there may indeed be a refugee situation involved. Once that conclusion is reached, the person proceeds to a two-person oral hearing where the decision is made on whether the person is a refugee. That is in accordance with the committee's report.
The Hon. Member raised the issue of the safe third country concept. The presence of a list is a notion that I have heard through a lot of testimony and conversations I have had both formally and informally. Let me use the analogy of the Post Office. When it decides that it wants a postal rate increase, it asserts to Cabinet that it wants the rate to be a certain amount. Cabinet can agree or disagree with the rate, but cannot change it.
I have a certain sense of comfort in having a single expert body in this country that becomes the definitive recommending group. I suggest that the committee would want to look very carefully at that part of the Bill. The one body in this country that will acquire the expertise, have the research resources and have the concern will be the Convention Refugee Determination Board. I would have confidence if it decided that a certain country was safe for nationals of another country.
The voters need a monitoring system and it is probably wise to provide for Cabinet approval. We need to study this area more closely to make sure that in the use of that list, discretion still remains with the officer, because situations change overnight in this field and discretion must exist. However, the list itself must be one in which the board has confidence. If not, we are running some risk of having the wrong kind of morality. That is my view of how to deal with the third country concept.

May 12, 1987
Adjournment Motion

Mr. Speaker, I will not comment on my regard for the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes). He and others know of my respect for him.
However, I will ask him to take a further look at pages 13 and 14 of the Bill, particularly Clause 48.1(1), which states:
A person who claims to be a Convention refugee is not eligible to have the claim determined by the Refugee Division if . . .
It goes to list (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e). Clause 48.1 (l)(b) states:
... the claimant came to Canada from a country that has been prescribed as a safe third country-
This morning, the Minister seemed to think that (b), like (a), is somehow qualified or modified by 48.1(2), but that is not so. That applies only to 48.1 (1 )(a). It makes an exception for somebody who is found to be a refugee in another country and now thinks he has to flee that country as well. Although that person comes from a country that we call safe, he would have his claim determined as a refugee from that country. Section 48.1(1 )(b) is not given any kind of qualification or exemption as is in 48.1(2).
On page 14 of the Bill, Clause 48.1(4) states:
In determining whether a claimant has a credible basis for the claim to be a Convention refugee, the adjudicator and the member of the Refugee Division shall consider any evidence adduced at the inquiry or hearing regarding-
In other words, that is all they can consider. According to 48.1 (4)(a), they can look at the record that Canada makes with respect to human rights of the country that the claimant left, or outside of which the claimant remains, by reason of fear or persecution, in other words, whether the country has a good or bad human rights record.
Clause 48.1 (4)(b) states:
The disposition-
That is by Canada:
-under this Act or the regulations of claims to be Convention refugees made by other persons who alleged fear of persecution ...
In other words, whether Canada found any refugees from that country before. That is the only criterion they can consider under that subclause. They are not allowed to consider the explanation of an individual. They can only consider the record of the country, its human rights record, and the experience of whether there have been previous refugees from that country.
As the Hon. Member said, the situation can change overnight, but the person is out of luck in that case. There have been no refugees from France, so if the Fascists took over France and Mitterand had to run to Canada, he would not be a refugee because we never had any refugees from France before.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for raising some of the clauses on pages 13 and 14 because those are clauses which concern a great many people across the country. In my eight years in Parliament, I have heard Ministers stand in the House and indicate Cabinet's intention by saying: "There is a sense of solidarity in Cabinet. This is our intention". I have been to legislative committees and other kinds of committees from time to time where when one looked at the fine print and found, there was a discrepancy between Cabinet's intention and the exact wording which came out of a process of drafting, and so on.
I was with the Hon. Member when we looked at the most recent amendments to the Immigration Appeal Board. We were able to achieve some very substantial and important amendments which I think have been helpful to the functioning of that board. I have heard with clarity in more than one Question Period and in the speeches today that it is the intention of Cabinet that the Members present at that first stage hearing will having discretionary powers. If the fine print in some way obviates that discretionary power, makes it impossible to exercise, we not only have to find that this is a problem but we have an obligation to suggest a solution which gets the job done.
Standing here in this Chamber today, not being a lawyer, I cannot find the solution. However, I hope that there are a lot of people around the country looking for the problems and then going to the next stage and asking: "Is there a solution to that problem?" I think in many cases, and in this case in particular, it is possible to find the problem and it is relatively easy to correct it.
By hindsight we will know if we were successful but I think that is the commitment.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 66, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie)-Disasters- Anniversary of Chernobyl nuclear accident-impact on Canada-(b) Request for information; the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell)-Status of Women- Harassment of woman firefighter-(b) Request for payment of compensation: the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Red way)-National Defence-possible effect of closure of ports to nuclear powered ships.
May 12, 1987

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Marchi:
That this House condemns the Government's refugee policy for its failing badly to uphold Canada's proud and humane record for refugee assistance and for abandoning our nation's respected international leadership on this tragic, world-wide human dilemma, which will serve to jeopardize a meaningful international solution to what is clearly an international phenomenon;
That this House further deplores the Government's refusal to assure refugee claimants full accessibility to, and a non-adversarial hearing before, an independent refugee board, and
That, therefore, this House urge the Government to establish a fair, accessible and efficient refugee administration system which would:
(1)	guarantee full accessibility to the system for refugee claimants by rejecting any pre-screening stage within the process;
(2)	ensure maximum protection and safety for all refugees and a comprehensive and adequate hearing of their claims by abolishing the highly restrictive "safe third country" concept as an integral part of the refugee determination process; and
(3)	provide every refugee with the opportunity of an appeal before a competent and independent refugee body that would consider all facts and circumstances of the appellant's claims.

Mr. Speaker, in addressing this motion today, I would like to start by expressing the feeling of indebtedness felt by myself and my Party to the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) in bringing forth this very important question of significant, compelling and, indeed, urgent interest to all Canadians. Bill C-55 has been tabled for first reading on May 5 and we will all come to debate it in due course. However, I think it is good that we have the opportunity today to, in a sense, pre-debate the Bill by raising some of the questions to which those who have looked at it find no answers, and also to enable Members of the House to put on the record and before Canadians some of the concerns which groups who are active, involved and committed to the plight of refugees have expressed .
After all, we are debating something that relates to what 1 think we could describe as a Canadian tradition of great worth. 1 do not say it is a great tradition because, after all, it has not been a consistent theme. Without going into some of the faults and errors of the past, because I would not like them to be misinterpreted in some way as a partisan comment, 1 think we would have to say that the more recent history of Canada's attitude and actions towards refugees within the world community has merited some accolades, most significant of which has been the Nansen Medal.
The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), who has a record of commitment to this particular question throughout his years of service in this House, went to some length in talking about the proud record of Canadian policy and hospitality, the welcoming of those who have had to leave their countries through no fault of their
Supply
own but because they had the normal aspirations of freedom loving people everywhere. They were not able to exercise those aspirations within the confines of the countries in which they were brought up.
It is a proud and diverse record. Today Canada is home to the first generation of refugees from Chile, the fascist dictatorship of General Pinochet, from South Africa's apartheid regime, from the frightful oppression of the B'hai in Iran and the equally frightful oppression of those who supported opposition Parties. Canada is host to refugees from the lawlessness and murder in Guatemala and El Salvador, and from the genocide in what was previously known as Cambodia. It is also host to people who fled oppression in Vietnam, from Laos, and to people of Ukrainian, Hungarian and, more recently, Polish origin, who originally came to this country as refugees.
When I hear talk of Canada's refugee determination system having been abused, I become very uncomfortable because while it is perfectly true that there may be those who have abused the system in the past, I think we would have to say that this country as a whole has never been abused by refugees, as I am aware of Canadian history. Even if there have been some who have, so to speak, beaten the system in order to gain entry to the country, I do not think it could be said that after having done so, they abused Canada.
It should be a mark of pride for all Canadians to be awarded the Nansen Medal which, I would stress, did not go to the Government of Canada but to the people of Canada. It should be a mark of pride which we as Canadians should maintain in the face of some of the confusion which exists and which, I regret to say, is at times promulgated regarding the situation of refugees and particularly in terms of refugees as juxtaposed with immigrants.
There have been some nostrums peddled in this country which are false and which have gained some credibility. They are deserving and, and indeed, demanding of refutation in this House. I will go into the details later. We have seen in recent years a wilful confusion at times and at other times an innocent confusion between the situation of refugees and immigrants. We have seen allegations, almost universally disproven or unsubstantiated, about the possible effects of refugees on employment in Canada. That was very well refuted in the speech of the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East. We have seen refugees used as a proxy target, as strawmen, by those who frankly are concerned to promote and promulgate racist theories, attitudes and practices. We have also seen a very legitimate concern, one which I think history and our experience very adequately answers, regarding the country's ability to absorb newcomers.
As one of those absorbed newcomers myself, I can hark back-although not from personal experience, obviously-to the year 1910 when approximately 400,000 immigrants, many of whom under today's system would be categorized as refugees, came to a country of some seven million or eight million people. We only have to go to our prairie and western

provinces today to see the success of these people and their descendants who have grown into a very lively, vital and integral part of Canadian society and, indeed, our Canadian identity.
Government policy has been outlined recently in the Government's response to petitions which some Members have presented in the House concerning Canada's refugee policy. It is worth quoting the Government's response to the petitions and recalling to Hon. Members on the government side and to Ministers what was said. I quote directly from the answer which states:
There are three components to Canada's refugee policy. First, there is the assistance which is provided through the United Nations High Commission for Refugees that includes aid to refugees, technical assistance to the UNHCR, and diplomatic initiatives to deal with the root causes of refugee situations.
Parenthetically, that is obviously not the subject of today's motion.
Second, there is the program of government and private sponsorship of refugees abroad who can best be helped by resettlement in this country. Third, there is the protection, which we guaranteed when we signed the Geneva Convention and Protocol, against the return of any refugee on Canadian soil to a territory where he would fear persecution on the basis of his race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.
I quote further an element of trumpeting which the Government provided in its response:
While Canada has established excellent standards of refugee status determination, it is recognized that there is a need to streamline our procedures which have broken down in the face of increasing volumes. There is a need to overhaul the way we deal with people who arrive spontaneously at our borders. To this end, the Government will be bringing legislation before the House shortly.
That, of course, refers to the legislation which the Government has brought forward in Bill C-55.
Because Canada has undertaken solemn international obligations to protect a person who is out of his or her country and unable to return because of fear of persecution on account of political, religious, or the other reasons mentioned, I think that it would behove the Government to consult the UNHCR which is, in a sense, the custodian of the Geneva Convention and Protocol. Let us be sure that within the forum of those who have also signed this Protocol any measures that Canada brings in to change its policy and procedures are determined to be in compliance with the Protocol. I do not think there could be any greater disgrace within the international community than having a country whose citizens won the Nansen Medal see its Government undertake a change in policy which might essentially nullify the validity and the commitment of the signature on that Protocol and Convention.
1 do not think there is argument within the House that the system proposed in the present legislation is more simple than the one it replaces. What we have to discuss is, of course, is it more fair? Indeed, is it as fair as we as Canadian legislators can make it under the circumstances?
The proposed system contrasts the eight steps of the existing system with a three-step process. It would be hard to argue that that is a more complex process than what is in place at the moment. But we have to determine if there are improvements that can be made in the interests of fairness. Having a simple system is simply not good enough for a country that can take some legitimate pride in its past record.
I would now like to deal with some of the problems that we perceive with Bill C-55 as presently drafted. Obviously, we do so not in an attack on the Government but in an attempt to have the Government address these concerns and modify the legislation accordingly.
We feel that there is an aura of inaccessibility about the procedures that are proposed. Instead of ensuring that everyone who arrives in Canada claiming to be a refugee gets his or her claim heard, there is some sense that the return to another country might be what they should expect if they want a realistic assessment of their prospects. The use of technicalities in some artificial categories, such as the safe third country category, also brings into question the intent of the Bill.
The initial screening, which can only be appealed from out of the country, proposes a bureaucratic barrier which, in the past, has jeopardized the safety of some refugee claimants. It has led to frustration and an enormous expense and effort on the part of refugee claimants for a consideration that we do not feel really warrants that sort of stress being put on refugee claimants.
Apparently, the second stage oral hearing can be appealed, but only to the Federal Court and only on matters of law as opposed to matters of fact. That is a grave deficiency because, surely, in a refugee determination process it is the facts of the case of the individual refugee claimant which should govern.
Where are the provisions for humanitarian or compassionate consideration such as those found in the current legislation? About 12 per cent of the current cases that do not meet the technical situation, the technical definitions, are situations in which compassionate people such as cabinet Ministers are willing to allow refugee claimants to stay in the country. I think that is something that the Government has to consider.
I would like to talk, and I hope at not too great a length, about the concept of safe third country, because I feel that in some ways it is a dangerous one and, in many ways, a very sensitive one. First, we know that the definition of safe third country is something that, on the enactment of the Bill, will be expropriated by senior bureaucrats in the Department of Immigration. We know that the individual adjudicator or member of the board will not have control over the definition of what is a safe third country. He or she will not have control over the designation of a safe third country. Therefore, it is a concept that will be bureaucratized and centrally controlled. One would assume, because such is the habit of bureaucracies, that it will be applied rigidly.
Obviously, this concept would require some form of return agreement with other countries, otherwise there would be no

right to send refugee claimants back. I think that one of the situations that concerns us the most is that of the Salvadorans and Guatemalans who have taken refuge in the United States and who now, because of increasing crack-downs in that country on migrant workers and those who do not have legal status, are seeking to come to Canada.
The United States declares and proclaims that the Governments of El Salvador and Guatemala are democratic, humanitarian and able to defend human rights within their countries. It is not my purpose to inveigh against the Governments of either of those countries where we know there are honest, dedicated and committed people trying their best to preserve an orderly democratic system of government. However, they do so in the face of militarism and in the face of an entrenched elite that is not willing to give up its power and that is willing to use extra-legal, military and terrorist means to maintain that power, even in the face of the best intentions of the Governments of those countries.
So that if we are considering the case of a Salvadoran refugee under the new legislation and this person is told: "Well, the United States is a safe third country", and Canada sends that person back to the United States, we would be somewhat in the situation, as a country, of a Pontius Pilate. We would not deport a person ourselves but we would send him back to another country that we could be perfectly sure would deport him.
This phenomenon, this risk of what we might call onward deportation, of deporting refugee claimants for onward deportation back to their own countries, is a serious issue that I certainly hope a government Member will address. I certainly hope a government speaker will address the issue. I also hope that it will be adequately addressed in the legislation as it is finally passed in the House after we have had an opportunity to process appropriate amendments through committee.
Obviously there is an element of politicization in terms of the safe third country concept. Obviously Canada, in the application of that concept, will be subjected to potential political or diplomatic pressures regarding the application, the definition, and the designation. After all, what will be the situation if one of our major trading partners involved in a trade deal or, shall we say, a major purchase of Canadian wheat or Canadian aircraft was told ever so subtly by government representatives that the commercial interchange was dependent upon Canada not designating their country as being an unsafe third country or not saying that their country was a country which could produce refugees? I think it would not strain the imagination or recollection of most Hon. Members of the House to determine and identify some of the potential examples.
We have some major criticisms of the screening process. The no credible basis for claim is something that is not defined. It is new legal language and lacks a specific definition. The

obvious example would be somebody coming as a refugee from a country which has not in the past been known to produce refugees. Therefore, it is a definition which would put in jeopardy some of those potential immigrants.
In conclusion, we cannot allow the confusion to continue between immigrants and refugees, understanding the distinction as an important part of understanding the concerns which our Party and members of all Parties want to put forward today. After all, spectres are being raised, and I am sure the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) did so unwittingly when he talked about thousands of bogus claimants in the queue.
I believe that Canada has only deported 600 or 700 people as bogus refugee claimants. We cannot confuse the immigrant strain who, after all, are generally queued up at Canadian consulates and delegations overseas with the refugee strain who, if they are queued, are queued at points of entry into the country.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your tolerance and consideration in hearing the problems today. They are problems which we want to see the Government address, so that the country will have a refugee determination system, of which we can all be proud.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member on his comments and to ask him about a particular point.
He referred to the total absence in the Bill of any possibility of providing the kind of humanitarian consideration currently provided in the legislation which the Bill is supposed to amend. In the decisions that will be made at the first stage, if they found that a person had no credible basis of claim or that a person came from a so-called safe country, the person would then be returned according to the Act. Of course that could include many people such as Iranians and others whom we do not now force to return to their home country.
Would the Hon. Member enlarge a little on that point? Since I know he has a world-wide concern and he has made reference to it, would he enlarge upon the difficulty of seeing where there is any fair treatment for such people within the present proposals, given the screenings?
First, they cannot even arrive here if they come from a country from which we require a visa or a transit visa. If they are refugees, they will probably be denied it. I know that the Canadian Government has specifically named Chile as a country to be impacted upon for having sent refugees here under transit visas.
Second, if they come from a country which does not produce refugees, they will be excluded in Section 48(a). The third example would be those who passed through and stayed in a safe country.
Could the Hon. Member comment upon how he thinks people would get the kind of humanitarian considerations we have been giving them now?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), not only for his question but for his outstanding commitment to this issue over a number of years.
In reply I should like to return to the Government's response to petitions and instance some examples which would fall through what we might say is the safety net of the Geneva Convention. I believe these examples provide compelling reasons for there to be included in the Act provision for ministerial discretion on humanitarian and compassionate grounds. I should like to quote again from the Government's response to petitions as follows:
-there is the protection, which we guaranteed when we signed the Geneva
Convention and Protocol, against the return of any refugee on Canadian soil to
a territory where he would fear persecution on the basis of his race, religion,
nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.
Let us look at three examples. I choose the examples of a Lebanese woman, of an Iranian young man, and of a Chinese woman. Let us consider that an 18-year old Iranian arrives in Canada and claims to be a refugee because in his own country he would be conscripted into the army, or one of the irregular fighting units prevalent in the Iran-Iraq war, and sent to the front where there are mortality rates in individual units of 50 per cent to 70 per cent and where the rates run higher in the case of young boys in their early teens who are used as human minesweepers and sent into Iraqi minefields to be blown up in order to clear a path for the troops. I do not see that the present legislation would allow in an Iranian who was attempting to avoid conscription for a war in which he would essentially be used as a completely disposable fighting individual in the cause which they are pursuing against Iraq.
Let us take the example of a Chinese woman who flees to Canada because she is in her second pregnancy and the Government of that country not only frowns on but takes some concrete and somewhat repressive measures against people who choose to expand their families. Where is there provision in the legislation which would allow that woman to be granted refugee status in Canada?
Finally, let us consider the situation of a woman in Beirut who, after all, wants to get away from the fighting. We saw a report in our newspapers a couple of months ago of a Beiruti who was willing to sell his eight children to anyone who would take them to a safe country. It is an indication of the level of desperation in some people trying to escape what is essentially a war zone. Could the person claim that he was being individually persecuted on any of the grounds of the Geneva Convention? He could not, but the fact is that the bullet from a Kalashnikov makes no such distinction. When a person is in peril of his life because he is in a war zone then obviously he has to be treated as a refugee and obviously he should be treated as a refugee in making application to Canada.
These would be examples that I feel, Mr. Speaker, the legislation must address. We must have measures in Bill C-55
to allow people to qualify and be treated as legitimate refugees, admissible to Canada on those grounds.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to take part in this debate this afternoon. I have enjoyed very much the comments of my colleagues who have preceded me. This is a very important subject and it is one that has seen many issues raised on which we have had a good dialogue. I would like to commend all my colleagues who have participated and who will participate in the debate.
Proposals for a new refugee determination system have been tabled in Parliament. They establish a system which reinforces Canada's commitment to genuine refugees in fear of persecution. The new system has a number of features which provides significant rights to refugees. These rights are consistent with our obligations under the United Nations convention relating to the status of refugees and with the Canadian Charter of Rights. The system, above all, ensures that no genuine refugee will be returned to a country where he or she is in danger of persecution.
Canada is, and will continue to be, a place of safe haven for genuine refugees who need our protection. This system upholds our commitment, a long-standing commitment, which is a vital element of a policy which, since World War II, has enabled some 500,000 refugees to settle in Canada. The Government has tried to put in place a fair and compassionate structure that will admit genuine refugees and screen out those who make fraudulent claims.
The proposals for this new system represent substantial improvements over the existing one in a number of ways. I would like to touch on just a few, if I may. For example, arguable cases can be referred for determination within a few days, and decisions on refugee status can be made within months rather than years, as is now too often the case. I think this cures a very serious shortcoming in the existing system.
The new system provides a number of safeguards for the individual, including the right to legal counsel. This is very important. Legal aid will be provided where necessary. A safe third country list will be established by Cabinet, and Cabinet has indicated that it will give very careful consideration concerning that list. I think some of our colleagues who have participated in the debate today, notably the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) and the response from the Minister highlight and underscore the importance which this provision has and the importance of our giving very careful consideration to the legal interpretations so that we can make a very valuable contribution in committee.
A new refugee board will be made up of members with specialized training in refugee matters. The new refugee board will also have the resources to deal with claims quickly for the benefit of refugees who need our protection. Of course, every claimant will have the right to appeal by leave to the Federal Court on questions of law. This new system will support a fair immigration program of moderate controlled growth that will

benefit all Canadians. While we continue to have an open immigration policy and need the talents and skills that new immigrants will bring, we want to be able to manage our system in a way that better serves all refugees and all Canadians.
The new legislation will also allow us to focus our resources on overseas selection of refugees. There are some 10 million to 12 million people still in refugee camps throughout the world. That is a matter we should keep before us when considering important resolutions like this one and important Bills like the one tabled in the House.
This year Canada will welcome some 125,000 new immigrants. This figure is up from the target of 115,000 in 1986 and up from the 85,000 to 90,000 people who were admitted in 1985. The figure is also up from the 84,000 people admitted in the year we took office. It should be noted that our Government has taken giant strides forward in this area and we have had the courage to grapple with some very serious problems.
In every respect this new legislation is intended to protect the rights of genuine refugees so that anyone needing Canada's protection will not be turned away. This new system preserves the integrity of our over-all program, which includes mechanisms to discourage queue jumpers and to deal effectively and swiftly with people who circumvent the normal legal channels. It also serves better genuine refugees and those applying to join our Canadian family. New Canadians have made a great contribution to Canada, and under this legislation we are confident they will continue to do so.
An important aspect of immigration which I believe we all support and on which I would like to touch in passing is that of family reunification. These proposals do not compromise our commitment to family reunification. On the contrary, I feel that a managed and controlled immigration policy allows us to direct resources to family reunification in greater measure.
New Canadians contribute to every phase of Canadian life. We need new Canadians. We want them and we welcome them. I am hoping that this new system we are trying to put in place will speed their entry into Canada and discourage any of those who would impede their entry by making fraudulent claims or by trying to get ahead of the process and short-circuit the system. That is the purpose of the new measures, and that purpose is a worthy one which deserves our support. I believe that all of us want to see our country continuing to grow. We want to share the good things which Canada has to offer with all new Canadians. The more we are able to accommodate, the better and the happier we will all be. Thank you for allowing me to intervene in the debate, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I treat today's debate as one of the most important debates in which I have participated in this session of Parliament. I think there is no issue that demands more concern on the part of Members of Parliament than an issue that quite literally deals with life and death matters.
It has been said that one of the highest tests of a nation is how it treats its least well off citizens, the poor, the disabled and the disadvantaged. I propose an equally high test, which is how a nation treats those who are not its own citizens but find themselves in desperate circumstances, needing compassion and help from those able to provide it. That is what we are debating today. Is this nation living up to its fullest and best potential in helping those least able to help themselves? The clear answer is no.
What disturbs me most is that the legislation that has been introduced by the Government is a major alteration in an evolutionary pattern that began in 1951 with the signing of the Geneva Convention. After that, a series of steps were taken by successive Governments to improve, enlarge and enhance the capacity of the Canadian Government to respond to the refugee issue. We heard many horrific tales about great swarms of people trying to beat down the doors of Canada. I listened to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) exploit those numbers by trying to raise the fear that there would be a great flood of people.
In the last 30 years, Canada has accepted over 400,000 refugees. We have accepted more refugees per capita than any other country in the world. During that period of time, we began to lead the world in the way we dealt with refugee problems. Our record was not unblemished but it was always improving. It was always taking that extra step based upon a compassionate appeal, not upon an enforcement appeal.
What is so disturbing to those of us who have been personally and directly involved in refugee matters for many years is that this Government is breaking that tradition. This Government has turned its back on that tradition. It does not show the most compassion possible and is now following the pack. It is not attempting to build a consensus for a greater reception and treatment of refugees. Instead, it is turning the screws and saying that we must exploit our worst biases. That is the problem.
It was not always so. When I inherited the post of Minister of Employment and Immigration, a good series of initiatives had been taken by the Government of the former Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), on Indo-Chinese refugees. A sponsorship program for private citizens had been offered and we doubled that program and accepted well over 100,000 Indo-Chinese refugees between 1978 and 1982, perhaps the most exemplary record of any country in the world.
We tend to forget that Canada's refugee-determination procedure is quite new. It only really began in 1978 with the passage of the new Act. It was up to successive Governments to build around that legislation a policy, a program and an administration that would give life to the spirit of the legislation.
If Members would read the debates that occurred in this House for close to two years during the enactment of that legislation, they would find it very instructive because they would understand that the key to making an effective refugee policy work is bringing Canadians on side, working with the churches, working with non-governmental organizations, and providing leadership that would bring out the best in Canadians. Through that partnership, we are able to show an incredible amount of generosity and openness.
Rather than trying to build a consensus for a more open, tolerant and compassionate refugee policy, this Government, for reasons which are hard to understand, has turned in the other direction. Instead, it is trying to show leadership against refugees.
Time and again, I have heard the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration say that a genuine refugee would never be turned away. If that is the case, why is the safe country clause in the legislation? Because the Minister is in the House, I would like to pose an interesting proposition to him. Will the United States of America be considered a safe country? I presume it will be. It is a close ally and a democratic country. It meets all the so-called criteria on which one would judge a safe country.
Let me deal with some interesting statistics from last year. In the United States, the chance of a refugee claimant from El Salvador or Guatemala being accepted was about 2 per cent. For those from Poland, it was 49 per cent, and for those from Iran, it was 66 per cent. What is clear is that the refugee determination procedure in the United States is infused with the political and ideological objectives of the Reagan administration. For one who comes from Central America, the United States is not a safe country.
I can say from personal experience, having been in refugee camps in El Salvador, Honduras and Guatemala to witness what is going on there, that when those people are sent back to their countries, which is what happens under the so-called safe country policy, they are condemned to prison, to intimidation and to threat. That is the conundrum the Government has created with this legislation. It is attempting to tell Canadians not to worry about refugees because it has a list of safe countries.
Can anyone tell me that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will tell his friend, the President, that the United States is not a safe country for refugees? Of course he will not say that. We know, however, from the facts, that it is not a safe country for refugees from Central America.

That is not new information. The Mennonite Central Committee and the coalition of church groups have told the Government time and time again that if it attempts that kind of pre-screening it is going to get itself involved in that kind of a dilemma.
What also bothers me a great deal is the attempt to suggest that somehow the Government was left with a mess and things were not being looked after. The Government knows that that was not the case. In 1981, we brought in new refugee guidelines. We set up the Refugee Status Advisory Committee as an independent organization. We established a task force to look at streamlining the refugee determination process. We established the Plaut Commission which came up with a series of recommendations. In other words, as the problem began to grow we responded. Those recommendations were on the table the day the Government took office. Two and a half years later it has rejected the proposals put forward by those independent groups and come up with its own made-in-the-department solution which emphasizes keeping people out, not providing the best way of bringing them in. All the Government had to do was to implement those proposals. However, because it was something the Liberal Government did, the Conservatives would not touch it. They wasted two and a half years, rejected the findings of a committee with a majority of Conservative Members, and now they have the nerve to say they inherited the problem. Of course there was a big problem, but a response was made.
Let me provide another small piece of history which may be constructive to this debate. At the beginning of 1982, in full recognition of a growing problem, that being the number of people who were trying to gain admission not only to Canada but to West Germany, the U.S., France, and all the other countries concerned at that time, the Government of Canada initiated a series of discussions beginning with the U.S. We then broadened it to include the Europeans, the Japanese and others in a series of international meetings designed to come up with an international approach to dealing with the refugee problem. We recognized that when one country closed its doors, that would create a problem for another country. So we started laying the groundwork for an agreement that would provide for a co-ordinated approach to the UNHCR. Each country could then follow the same pattern and we would make sure of an effective and co-ordinated allocation of responsibility.
What happened to that initiative? Why was it dropped? Recognizing that the UNHCR was not getting the necessary political motivation and that this country was being looked to for leadership, surely that initiative should have been followed through and built upon. Yet the Minister of Employment and Immigration said that his Government inherited the mess. What he inherited was a series of solutions which his Government rejected and discarded. I am surprised that even to this day there has been no attempt to resurrect that kind of
