international policy-making approach to the problem of refugees.
This past week-end I was at a round table discussion on Central America. It brought together people from Latin America, Central America, the U.S. and Europe to talk about how to deal with the incredibly tragic circumstances in Central America. It was both rewarding and instructive to hear the diplomats and political leaders of the various countries concerned repeating that Canada had a major role to play in that region. It was not a passive role, it was a major role. One of the errors they pointed to specifically was that of refugee policy. They pointed to the past initiatives we had taken for rescuing political prisoners from El Salvador and bringing them to Canada. We initiated a sanctuary program whereby someone who was being deported by the American authorities to Central America would be picked up and brought to Canada with the co-operation of church and refugee organizations. We were told that this kind of initiative established our reputation as well as trust and confidence in us in dealing with the most intractable problems in Central America.
Now we are erasing that and turning the clock back. Other countries were looking to us for leadership. They said we could make a valuable contribution in one of the trouble spots of the world. Yet, because of the initiatives taken in closing our borders last May and in this new legislation, we are foreclosing our options and refusing the opportunity to continue the initiative.
We have to ask ourselves why. It is not a partisan issue. No one is going to score any political points. Or are they? Is this something involving that kind of cynicism where you can pander to a bias out there and say, boy, we are getting tough?

I hear a comment from the lowest of the low. We have to consider the source.
What is the reason for this? If the Minister has an alternative reason, let us hear it. No rational reason has been given. No historical reason has been given. Clearly there are alternatives which are far more acceptable even to Conservative Members. One has to ask, why is the Government doing it? That is why we brought this legislation forward today. It is to try to focus the attention of Canadians on the fact that this is the wrong answer, the wrong approach.
There are other ways of handling the problem and streamlining the process. You can do it in a way that you do not strip people of their rights and liberties and turn your back on all those who look to this country for leadership and sanctuary.
That is why my colleague in his opening remarks said it is time Members opposite began to look at their conscience. They should begin considering how this legislation can be changed. It would not take much to turn it around. It would not take much to turn the legislation into something that is positive and useful. The first step would be to listen to the groups deeply

May 12, 1987
Supply
involved in the process. The Mennonite Central Committee and other church organizations, those who are working in the refugee camps, the non-governmental organizations, are all desperately opposed to this legislation. Surely that should tell the Government something. It should understand that if all those who have committed their lives and resources to work for and represent refugees are saying we are doing the wrong thing, it is about time the Government opened its ears and listened.
The proposals are not that difficult to deal with. The prescreening process is certainly the first and foremost thing that has to be changed. By doing that, the Government would begin to show some good faith It would begin to show that you can bring in a determination procedure which recognizes rights and does not close doors. It comes to grips with problems as they need to be addressed. In that way the Government would bring on board that great well-spring of compassion and interest which exists in so many of the organizations and individuals involved across this country. That is the same kind of good will that was tapped when we brought in the Hungarians and Ugandans, the Chileans and Indo-Chinese, and the Poles, when they were all having their problems. When we brought in tens of thousands of refugees Canadians were prepared to accept them. Those people have become very much a part of the Canadian community. They have become resettled. They have found a home here and are making an important contribution to Canada. We did ourselves proud by managing that problem.
O)
When the Government studies the evolution that has taken place since World War II, and particularly in the last 10 years during which Canada provided a standard of leadership and responsibility, it will recognize that what it has now done is wrong. Simply by admitting it is wrong and turning to a different course it can win the applause of everyone involved and begin to provide leadership so that those who are homeless can find a home.

Mr. Speaker, whenever 1 listen to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) 1 think back to the time when he was a Minister in the former Government. I think back to when he was responsible for employment and immigration. I listen to him with great care and I think of what he did when he was responsible for that portfolio. I have found some facts and figures which show that when the Hon. Member was the Minister of Employment and Immigration in 1981, we brought into this country just short of
15.000	refugees. In 1986, the Government brought almost
19.000	refugees into this country. In 1981-82, when the Hon. Member was the Minister, his Government spent $26,748,000 on international humanitarian assistance. In 1985-86, the last fiscal year for which we have figures, the Government spent $53,300,000 on international humanitarian assistance. In 1982, the Member's Government spent $30,435,000 on
settlement for refugees. In 1986, the Government spent almost $50 million on settlement for refugees.
There seems to be quite a difference between the money spent on settlement when the Member was a Minister in the former Government and the dollars which were spent by the present Government in the most recent years for which figures are available. There has been quite a substantial increase in the amounts spent. There has been quite a substantial increase in the amounts spent on international humanitarian assistance as well. There has also been quite a substantial increase in the number of refugee landings in this country from the time when the Member was a Minister in charge of these matters.
This makes me wonder just how sincere the Member is and whether he is speaking from his heart or whether he is not only, as suggested by his former colleague, the Hon. Donald Macdonald, engaged purely in political posturing. Is that what the Hon. Member is doing today? The figures from the time when the Member was a Minister do not stack up very well against those of today. Is he engaged in purely political posturing?

Mr. Speaker, every time I hear the Member for York East (Mr. Redway) ask a question I am reminded of the time when he was the Mayor of the Municipality of Metro Toronto and came to me, as Minister of Employment and Immigration, asking for assistance in setting up a youth employment program which the previous Government did. I am glad to say that the program became a highly successful model for the youth job corps.
The Member seemed to have an awful lot more common sense at that time than he seems to exhibit now. I was very pleased to work in partnership and co-operation with him at that time in establishing major programs in his municipality.
The Member asks about sincerity. He saw examples of that sincerity when he asked for assistance with the problem he was facing. One of the problems which he faced in his municipality at that time related to visible minorities. Many of those who had come into his municipality through immigration programs did not have opportunities for retraining and employment. The pilot program which we designed was established to meet that problem. Unfortunately, many of the programs which we initiated have been erased under the Canadian Jobs Strategy. I suppose if we were guilty of anything, it was of being too softhearted with various mayors of municipalities at that time.
With regard to the statistics which the Member quoted, we must factor into the equation the difference of seven years. Over that time there has been inflation, which changes figures. Only about 2,000 or 3,000 people applied for refugee determination in that year. It was only natural that the available money was spent to meet that need. We are saying that as the numbers grow, the resources have to be increased.
Over the last two years, the Department has not been living up to those expectations. It has not even been applying the instruments which are available under the present Immigration Act and its regulations. The backlog has been allowed to grow
May 12, 1987

because the proper assessments and judgments have not been made and people who are not legitimate refugees have not been asked to leave. The Government has been stalling. It has been dragging its feet on this issue. We must ask whether it is doing so in order to create the impression that there is a backlog.
Members talk about the problem of people coming from Portugal and Brazil. Why was there not some sort of visa control? We used such provisions from time to time. We did so when we were faced with the question of the Sikhs in 1982 who were making manifestly unfounded claims. The Government has not been taking such measures.
I come back to the basic point that I do not think the Government has been trying to manage the issue or deal with the problem even under the present initiatives. We saw the problems on the horizon three or four years ago and responded by starting the oral hearings and putting the guidelines in place. Only three years after the legislation had been passed we did a major revision of refugee policy, put new measures in place, and started a major examination of the determination procedures.
It is now four years since those measures were put in place, and we are hearing a series of proposals which totally contradict the wisdom of those independent task forces. That is the real issue at stake.
If we are talking about political posturing, rather than trying to make those political posturing points, if the Hon. Member would take his powers of eloquence and persuasion that he used upon me when I got youth programs for him and used them on his Ministers and the Government to make alterations in the refugee program, he, I and everyone else in the country would be much happier.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), the former Minister of Employment and Immigration, who obviously spoke with passion and deep-felt emotion about the issue.
It has become very evident that the Government will try to market its new product, Bill C-55, to the clientele, the Canadian population, on the basis of curbing abuse. There are two curious aspects to that marketing scheme.
First, the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry correctly articulated the point that Canada will be one of the first countries to legislate the third safe country concept which will encourage other countries to do likewise and thereby set up, in the Member's words, a pinball or domino effect in which there will be an international corridor of locked and jammed doors, only aggravating the desperate situation of individual refugees.
On the other hand, during this administration there has been an increase in the number of schemes and, perhaps scams, perpetrated by unscrupulous lawyers attempting to get
Supply
refugees into the country through the front or back door. We can look, for example, at Lebanon, Turkey, Portugal and Brazil as well as other countries on the horizon.
This shows that inflexibility and rigidity is not the answer to curbing abuse. There is an interesting correlation, that the more severe and restrictive the policy, the greater desperation and fewer options are present for refugees throughout the world.
One comes to the conclusion that Canada is not doing itself any favours, nor doing any favours for the international community, in trying to come to grips with what is an international phenomenon that ultimately requires an international solution. Will the Hon. Member comment on those elements that I believe are very crucial in this debate and which should be brought to the attention of all Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, I will try to answer as succinctly as I can in the few minutes remaining. First, I believe the Hon. Member has pointed to a very important axiom. As I learned in the three and a half years during which I was responsible for that Department, the more one tries to restrict, the more there will be new channels found to get around those restrictions. Attempting to close the door simply means that cracks will be found in other places.
I predict that one of the consequences of the present Government's action will be to encourage and stimulate a much broader occurrence in illegal refugee immigration activities as people find other ways of moving around the system. Rather than ensuring that all those who apply are given the proper opportunity for a fair hearing and then dispatched quickly as recommended by various reports, we will see a much higher incident of illegal entry into this country.
Second, as I alluded to in my opening remarks, I am not rising to say to the Minister of State for Immigration that this is an easy problem. It is a profound, deeply complex problem. One of the answers that must be found is on the international level. It is clear that the United Nations High Commission for Refugees needs the assistance of member countries to give a new policy direction and response to this issue. That is something we began in 1982-83 when we convened those meetings of other host countries to discuss whether we could not find ways of sharing the responsibility since we had the great privilege of having great opportunities that many other people did not enjoy.
I can report that progress was being made toward finding some resolution among the various host countries on how to coordinate action and ensure there was a common approach that was based on the idea of an open door, and even letting many of the countries of origin deal with the problems beginning to emerge.
! do not know why that initiative was stifled when the new Government came to power. It would be worthwhile finding out why that very important development of a new international response to the growing refugee crisis was erased and why we retracted our leadership.

May 12, 1987
Supply
I say to the Minister, in closing, that it is not too late to resurrect that kind of initiative and begin putting it into effect. I think the intent of my colleague's motion and our interest in being here to speak to it is to encourage the Government to do that very thing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the motion before the House today, a motion with which I certainly cannot agree. I would like to give the House an overview of the Bill tabled by the Government, which provides for a new process for determining refugee status in Canada. I am firmly convinced that this Bill strikes the right balance between justice for refugees and an efficient immigration program.
The present Government wants moderate and controlled increases in immigration levels. In 1985, the total number of landed immigrants was 85,000, and this number increased to
100.000	in 1986. In 1987, this figure is expected to be between
115.000	and 125,000. As was stated by the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner), Canada's refugee program is based on a threefold approach, in accordance with the United Nations policy relating to refugees.
The first component consists of a refugee assistance program with a budget of over $170 million in 1986-87.

The second component is resettlement from abroad. This is in line with the United Nations' approach that for some, the only solution is resettlement in a country far away from their homeland. Voluntary return or local resettlement are considered the best options for most refugees. Canada's resettlement record is outstanding, with 18,000-plus refugees in 1986 and 500,000 since World War II.
The third element is the determination system in Canada. It is designed to help those who arrive looking for protection and have nowhere else to go. This determination system is under severe pressure. It can no longer respond to genuine refugees in need. Over the last few years, refugee claims have increased dramatically. Population pressures in the Third World have caused massive migrations to developed countries.
The Europeans have moved to control abuse of their systems. The United States recently took steps affecting thousands of illegal immigrants there. The spill-over from these events has now reached Canada.

There are 80 million people in the world who have left their homes, and 15 million are refugees. We must find solutions at the international level, and Canada is playing a leading role in seeking such solutions.
Mr. Speaker, in 1980, there were 1,600 claims in Canada. In 1986, that number rose to 18,000. The forecast for 1987 is 25,000.
Before dealing with the Bill and its provisions for claiming refugee status in Canada, we must first agree on some basic definitions of refugees and refugee claims.
What is the difference between a refugee and a refugee claimant? What is an economic migrant? People coming to Canada and claiming refugee status are refugee claimants. But a refugee claimant is not necessarily a genuine refugee. Many are economic migrants.
Canada respects the United Nations' definition of a Convention refugee. Briefly, this is someone who is outside his or her country and is unable to return because of a real fear of persecution based on race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular social group. As a signatory to the U.N. Convention, Canada must give protection to those who have no other safe haven.
Economic migrants come to Canada to improve their economic well-being. They want to avoid immigration selection abroad. They are the major source of false refugee claims in Canada.

They should and must file an application through the usual channels at Canadian embassies and consulates.
Mr. Speaker, last year, two of the five main source countries of refugee claimants in Canada were Portugal and Turkey. These are not source countries of refugees. There has been a obvious abuse of our process for determining refugee status. Canada's ability to protect genuine refugees is being undermined and the process appears to favour these fraudulent cases. The consistent support of Canadians for increasing immigration levels and aid to refugees is suffering as well.

I now wish to outline the objectives of the proposed new system for refugee determination in Canada. The new Bill respects Canada's values and humanitarian traditions. Its objectives are to protect genuine refugees in need, to process claims fairly and quickly, to curb abuse, and to manage resources effectively. It ensures that refugees and immigrants are treated fairly.
There are several key features. The new process is streamlined. Refugee determination is completed in months. Now it often takes years. It quickly sorts out arguable cases from clearly unfounded claims. The system provides quality oral hearings before independent, well trained refugee board members, and provides for appeals to the Federal Court. The Bill sets up a new immigration and refugee board. There are two sections; an immigration board dealing only with immigration matters, and a Convention Refugee Determination Board dealing exclusively with refugee claims.
May 12, 1987



I shall now deal with how the new process works. Step one. Upon arrival in Canada, the individual claims refugee status and the claimant appears before an adjudicator and a member of the refugee board. Individuals with a defensible claim and those whose case is in some doubt are directed to the refugee board.

People who will not go on to the refugee board include people with refugee status elsewhere and people who arrive from a safe country where they have a claim, or a reasonable opportunity to make one. They will be returned to these countries. However, people who have simply passed through another country on their way to Canada will not be affected on these grounds. People with unfounded claims, such as the Portuguese claim of persecution as Jehovah's Witnesses, will be returned to apply in their home country. Anyone who was previously rejected as a refugee claimant in Canada, and anyone subject to a removal order, will also not proceed to the board. None of these people need Canada's protection.
Important safeguards are built into this process. The refugee board member must agree with the decisions. People not referred to the board are removed. However, they can appeal by leave to the Federal Court even though they are outside Canada. If the appeal succeeds, the person will be brought back at Government expense. Everyone has the right to counsel. A lawyer will be provided, if needed.

Mr. Speaker, these bona fide refugees will never be sent back to a country where they fear persecution. The list of safe countries will be short and will be drafted by Cabinet. Considerations in establishing the list will be the record of these countries on human rights and on the way they protect refugees. Cabinet will seek the advice of reliable sources including the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, nongovernmental organizations and the new independent Refugee Board. Safe countries that do not have an unblemished record with respect to some of their nationals will not be eligible.
Claimants whose case has been referred to the refugee board must be given a firm date for a hearing within 10 days.
Step 2-At the refugee board, the claimant will be given a hearing before a jury of two. The claimant is entitled to counsel. The hearing will be held according to a non-adversarial formula. The claim will be accepted if approved by one of the members of the refugee board. The claimant will be given the benefit of the doubt.

Work permits can be issued at this point. Step three, claimants accepted by the board can apply for landing. If the claim is rejected, reasons must be given. The claimant has the right of appeal by leave to the Federal Court. Removal takes place only after appeals are decided.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, the new refugee determination system ensures that genuine refugees are protected. Every
Supply
claimant is seen by at least one member of the refugee board. Claims will be processed fairly and quickly. Refugee determination will be decided in months, not years. The new system responds quickly to abuse. People coming to Canada for reasons other than protection will be speedily removed. Workable procedures aim, above all, at giving protection to those who need it, not to those who do not.
There are three steps in the new system. The old system had eight. People will be referred to the refugee board in a matter of days. Determinations will be made in months. It now takes years. The new system will get rid of long delays and uncertainty for genuine refugees. Rejected claimants will be speedily removed.
The new system meets Canada's Convention obligations, respects the Charter and the Bill of Rights, maintains Canada's humanitarian tradition, and preserves the integrity of the immigration and refugee programs.
I wish to emphasize that Canada's refugee program measures up internationally. The new system has more safeguards than most refugee-receiving countries. Canada has a generous refugee aid program both at home and abroad.
Our best contribution is still resettlement from camps abroad. Many of the people in these camps have been there for years and have no other options. The Government sponsors thousands every year, and there is no limit on privately-sponsored refugees. The Government helps groups find refugees to sponsor, helps with language training and pays for other resettlement services.
I have personally worked hard to obtain support from the Canadian executive of the International Parliamentary Union to have the question of refugees placed on the fall agenda of the world-wide IPU conference to be held in Bangkok, Thailand. With the assistance of Senator Bonnell of the other place and the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), Canada has gained support from the European 12-plus group of which Canada is a member. As a result, the international responsibility for refugees will be debated by the IPU next fall when Canada hopes to play the role of chef de file.
Canada's respected humanitarian record will continue. The Government is committed to protecting genuine refugees. It is firm in its resolve to curb abuse and committed to increased immigration.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to my colleague who sits on the Immigration Committee, the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Oostrom). The Hon. Member spent a considerable amount of time during his allotted time in the debate dealing with the question of fraudulent applications and the suggestion that Canada should not offer any assistance to those who wish to come in through the back door and break our regulations. I do not think there is one Member of

May 12, 1987
Supply
Parliament or one political Party which suggests that fraudulent claims should be rewarded to the detriment of those who are genuine and legitimate claimants.
I wish to ask the Hon. Member this. Instead of talking about the visa position and about getting tough with legislation, which in the end will hurt and handicap genuine claimants as has been suggested throughout this debate, what does the Hon. Member think of the Government's inaction in terms of bringing a great deal of the source of the cancer of fraudulent claims to some type of order? What does he feel about individuals such as John Santos who has made some $600,000 at the very least, who owns a $50,000 Mercedes and who lives by the sea in Portugal on the proceeds of fraudulent and scandalous schemes which take advantage of many innocent individuals? What does he think when he sees scams in Portugal, Lebanon and Turkey going on unabated and the fact that the Government is missing a chance to send a strong signal by prosecuting these individuals and by making a legitimate example of what we will not tolerate? How does the Hon. Member reconcile that action in the face of increased fraudulent and unscrupulous activities? What does the Hon. Member think ought to happen vis-a-vis unscrupulous consultants?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) for his question. I do not find the proposed legislation very tough on the part of Government in terms of real refugees. I find it to be humanitarian. I think it will provide a faster process. It will provide a solution. These people will not be held in limbo for years, as was the case under the previous Government. I think we are speeding up the process so that people will know exactly where they stand within a very short period of time. I think it is unjustified to call this policy tough. I would rather call it humanitarian.
With respect to the second part of the Hon. Member's question concerning fraudulent applications, I think that the Government has been trying to gather evidence, and I have been trying to gather evidence, to convict fraudulent immigration consultants. If the Hon. Member has any solid evidence to bring forward so that the Government can convict these consultants, we would be only too pleased to have it since we are having some difficulty in obtaining real evidence to convict these consultants. As I have said, I have been trying to obtain some solid evidence on this matter. Some people who have come to Canada, in particular those from Portugal and other countries, have come forward. They want to help the Government to convict these fraudulent operators in order that their families back home will not be harassed.
I hope that the Minister of Immigration, in consultation with the Department of Justice, will allow these people to stay here for perhaps a year. I hope that they will be given a work permit so that they can give evidence to the Government in order to prosecute these fraudulent operators in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate today, although I am saddened by what is contained in Bill C-55. As we have listened to government Members rise one after another a theme is clearly coming out through the speech notes that they have prepared or have had provided to them. They have used words such as "stop abuse" and "curb abuse". As has been pointed out by some Hon. Members, there are no Members in the House who support the abuse of the process as it has been set up to this point. But for the Government to try to claim that the approach it is taking through Bill C-55 is somehow streamlining and making the process more fair and so on is simply not the case.
I listened with care to what members of the Opposition had to say in terms of this type of legislation being a method of pandering to ideological biases and to certain perceived unfairnesses in the system. 1 think that we can see not only in this piece of legislation but in others a theme coming forward from the Government. In terms of the pornography legislation, rather than dealing with kiddie porn and violence against women the Government has gone much further. It is attempting to reach out to those biases that are floating around within Canadian society in terms of the legislation. In relation to the return of capital punishment, again, we find the same type of tone and the same kind of theme. We see the same words reaching out to Canadians which seem to say: "Look, we are going to reduce crime. We will bring back capital punishment. We will reduce the number of sex offences with this pornography legislation. We will reduce the amount of abuse of Canada's immigration system in terms of refugees and economic migrants," as the Hon. Member who just spoke called them.
A lot of the concern that there is throughout Canada, and I am talking about both urban and rural areas, has been created by some Members who sit on the government side. There is a concern on the part of those Canadians who are waiting for family reunification, for relations or for friends to come from the country from which they have come. They have been led to believe, through a lot of what has been said by government Members in speeches that they have given and in articles that they have sent out, that the reason they are having to wait such a long time is that our Canadian officials throughout the world are somehow spending all their time on cases of abuse by refugees, economic migrants and others. The concern is that the legitimate aspirations of other Canadians to have a son, daughter, mother, father, uncle, other relative, or friend join them in Canada are being held in abeyance, because the system is fouled up with those who are abusing it and the Government, for some reason, is spending all its time and energy in dealing with abuses.
The Minister who spoke did not give us any statistics on abuse. None of the government Members gave us specific cases of abuse. We know that there have been some. However, to say that the legislation is required to stop that leads me to
May 12, 1987

feel that the Government is looking at the whole refugee matter in terms of numbers rather than in terms of real families and the real pain behind many of their cases. The Bill is designed to deal with numbers.
It is not just a merry-go-round. Some government Members have tried to make it sound as if some people have had to return to a safe third country and then come back for another process, that the federal Government pays for them to come back, and all this kind of thing. In fact, it is quite different, and I will come to that in a moment.
Who are the refugees? Who are they? Members of the House talk about different clauses of the Bill, different procedures, and so on. However, one Canadian in 50 living in Canada today, on May 12, 1987, came to Canada since 1945 as a refugee under the various and changing pieces of legislation Canada used to deal with refugees. Canada has had a good record in most areas in terms of dealing with refugees.
I should like to spend a moment on what exactly is in today's motion, what has been proposed by the Canadian Council of Churches, and why groups are working in Central America, in South America, and in other parts of the world to assist refugees who are trying to flee persecution in other political systems on the basis of race, religion, economic participation in the economy, and, most often, political involvement. In terms of refugees fleeing to Canada, certainly in terms of Central America and South America, in most cases they are fleeing from extreme right wing dictatorships. I hope as well to have time to come to the ideological bias we find in the concept of safe third countries.
However, let us look at the motion before the House. It is reasonably clear. In part it suggests that the Government establish a system which would:
(1)	guarantee full accessibility to the system for refugee claimants by rejecting any pre-screening stage within the process;
(2)	ensure maximum protection and safety for all refugees and a comprehensive and adequate hearing of their claims by abolishing the highly restrictive "safe third country" concept as an integral part of the refugee determination process;-
As other Hon. Members have pointed out, between 1983 and 1986 the United States only accepted 2 per cent of those claimants who were trying to obtain refugee status, particularly from countries like El Salvador, whereas Canada accepted almost 50 per cent of such claims.
The Government says that Cabinet will decide what is a safe third country. Any of us who have been around here for a while-and I have been here for the last eight years-knows that Cabinet will not have monthly or bimonthly meetings to decide which countries are safe third countries. It will come from within the system. This is where the ideological bias of the Government is being built into it.
I think we all know of the pressures which are brought by Governments in places like El Salvador, Guatemala, India, and other nations around the world to bear on the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), on other Ministers,
Supply
and on the Government of Canada. They ask: "Why did you let so and so come to Canada as a refugee?" They ask why we let certain groups into the country and about the numbers. Because they have a certain level of trade with us, they want us to slow down and make them remain in such and such a country. This sets up a whole new bureaucratic mechanism. As other Members have pointed out, should Canada move in the direction of starting to close doors to make the whole system less accessible and of saying that someone must return to country x or go from there to another country, it will force more and more bona fide refugees.
Let us pull the mask off these unknown refugees. Who are these people? Half a million bona fide Canadians came to the country as refugees. Who were they? Who was persecuting them? Why did they choose Canada? I have dealt with many refugee cases in my own constituency. Generally, when they arrive at the borders of Canada, at an airport, on a boat, or whatever, they have used the last of their resources. Very few refugees have an opportunity to sell their home or their car and casually board a Boeing 747 to fly to Canada. Very few of them can say that they will set up a business or do x, y, or z. It is a totally different situation.
Our refugee system and the legislation to deal with refugees face to face must be incredibly sensitive to the reality of what these people and their families have gone through. They fled the countries where they were born. They fled a political system. They fled the reality of the country in which they were living and tried to find a safe haven.
As the legislation is drafted, some of these people will simply come before an almost untrained officer, perhaps at a border crossing or at an airport. They might have to spend three hours or four hours at an airport after having come perhaps half way around the world and having been in all kinds of unsavoury situations from which they have fled. They are given a few moments of time, quite often after having arrived here as part of a busload of people.
As other Hon. Members have pointed out, 18,000 refugees arrived in Canada last year. The Government is sending out signals that there is abuse and indicating the reasons one's grandmother cannot come from Scotland is the refugee problem, the abuse which has been created by the Liberals, the abuse in the system, and so on.
We must understand that the Bill was not drafted by the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner). Those of us who have been around here for a while know that pressure was brought from within the system. Are we really to say to Salvadoran refugees that the United States is a safe country?
Let us look at the evidence given before a Senate hearing in the United States. It is shocking. In testimony before a Senate subcommittee in April, 1985, the American Civil Liberties Union found evidence that returnees were abducted, murdered, beaten, and arrested. It also indicated that the United States only granted asylum to 2.6 per cent of those who applied between June, 1983 and January, 1986.

May 12, 1987
Adjournment Debate
We know that the Government is trying to curry favour with the United States Government on free trade and all kinds of other issues. The Government would not want to say to the United States: "You are not a safe country". If the Minister of State for Immigration were serious, why would he not indicate that Parliament or a committee of Parliament would determine the safe countries? It has been left to Cabinet.
What grounds are there for the Government to refuse to accept the proposal put forward by the Canadian Council of Churches? What could be more practical and more reasonable than its five points? They read as follows:
Refugee claimant arrives at border. Immigration Official registers person and refers to the Refugee Board. Claimants cannot be returned.
Claimant makes an appointment with Refugee Board for an oral hearing within a fixed time period after referral.

Claimant and legal counsel present case to a two person panel of competent specialized persons of a Refugee Board who will decide whether or not they believe the person is a refugee.
Stage 4 is the appeal/review, and Stage 5 is the Federal Court. Why did the Government not go that route?
The Government wants to create the belief among Canadians that there has been abuse, that the entire system is sort of stalled, that there cannot be family reunification and so on because of the ongoing process.
I know the Minister is a compassionate person. He must return to the drawing board. The "safe third country concept" simply must go. Other substantive changes must be made to the Bill.
To this point in time we have been a beacon of fairness around the world in terms of dealing with bona fide refugees. None of us support the abusers, the economic migrants, and so on. However, the Bill falls short of what all Canadians support, that is, a true sense of fairness in dealing with refugees from around the world.
I am sorry I do not have more time. I look forward to participating in the debate again.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It being 6 p.m., it is my duty to inform the House that pursuant to Standing Order 82(12), the proceedings on the motion have expired.
